title: Christ Before Bethlehem: Preexistence in Paul

keyTerms.d: That in Paul’s letters Christ is not a man who began at his birth and was later exalted, but one who existed before he came. That is a narrower claim than full deity, and it should not be inflated into one: preexistence is a step toward the deity of Christ, not identical with it.

Paul never sets out to prove that Christ preexisted; he assumes it, in the offhand way a writer treats settled common ground. The conviction surfaces as a shape pressed into letter after letter: sent from the Father, rich before he was poor, in the form of God before he took a servant’s, the agent through whom all things were made — a descent and a return, not the elevation of a man who began at Bethlehem.

“The form of God” and “the form of a servant” (Philippians 2:6–7). The word morphē is the hinge: the same noun describes what he became — a servant — and his servanthood was no costume, so the “form of God” he began in is equally real.

The Greek names no thing of which Christ emptied himself — grammatically he emptied himself by taking the form of a servant, by adding humanity, not by subtracting deity (Fee). Not that he set aside, lost, or diminished his deity: he remained what he was and became what he was not.

Christ as the one “through whom are all things” (1 Corinthians 8:6) and by whom “all things were created” (Colossians 1:16). Whatever else creation-agency implies, it requires that the agent not be among the created things — the one through whom the world was made stands, by the logic of the claim, before and outside it.

The reading of the Philippians hymn as a contrast between two men: Adam, made in the image of God, grasped at equality with God and was condemned to death; Christ, the last Adam, faced the same archetypal choice, refused to grasp, obeyed unto death, and was exalted. On this reading the hymn need not assert that Christ personally existed before Bethlehem. It is the most serious challenge, and it is argued from the text, so it is answered on the text.

The word marks priority and rank, not manufacture. Scripture uses it that way of David — “I will make him the firstborn, the highest of the kings of the earth” (Psalm 89:27) — though David was the youngest of Jesse’s sons. “Firstborn of all creation” names Christ’s supremacy over creation. And the very next verse blocks the created-being reading: “for by him all things were created” (Colossians 1:16).

Set side by side, the texts form a single arc that no one text has to carry alone. The weight rests not on any single uncontested proof-text but on the cumulative pattern, and on the named person — sent, made poor, crucified, raised — who is its subject throughout.

derive.q: “God sent forth his Son, born of woman” (Galatians 4:4) — the sending is named before the birth. So the word “sent” is…?
derive.ans: suggestive — but not, taken alone, proof
derive.why: Taken alone, “sent” need not imply preexistence — prophets are “sent” too, and the honest reader grants it. But notice the sequence in Galatians: God sent his Son, and the Son was then “born of woman.” The sending is named before the birth, which reads awkwardly if the sending simply is the birth of an ordinary man. The weight falls on the cumulative pattern, and on that sequence.

derive.q: “Though he was rich, yet for your sake he became poor” (2 Corinthians 8:9) — so the sentence…?
derive.ans: presupposes a wealth held before the becoming
derive.why: The logic is a transition from a prior state: he was rich, and became poor. A man who was born poor did not “become” poor for anyone’s sake. It faces its own skeptical reading — a metaphor of earthly self-impoverishment — which is why the weight falls on the cumulative pattern.

derive.q: “In the form of God… taking the form of a servant… born in the likeness of men” (Philippians 2:6–7) — the same noun, morphē, for both forms. So the “form of God”…?
derive.ans: is equally real — and the sequence is a transition
derive.why: The same noun describes what he became — a servant — and his servanthood was no costume, so the “form of God” he began in is equally real. And the sequence — in the form of God, then taking a servant’s form, then born in human likeness — describes a transition from one condition to another.

derive.q: “One Lord, Jesus Christ, through whom are all things” (1 Corinthians 8:6) — so the agent of creation…?
derive.ans: is not among the created things
derive.why: Whatever else creation-agency implies, it requires that the agent not be among the created things — the one through whom the world was made stands, by the logic of the claim, before and outside it. Paul places this preexistent one on the Creator’s side of creation.

derive.q: Grant the whole downward arc. Does preexistence, by itself, prove that Christ is God?
derive.ans: no — it is a step toward his deity, not identical with it
derive.why: Preexistence alone does not say what kind of being preexisted — some scholars hold that Paul’s Christ was an exalted angel — which is why the creation texts matter: they place this preexistent one on the Creator’s side of creation, and the one by whom every created thing was made cannot himself be one of the created things. The full case that he is included in the identity of the one God is made in the divine-identity essays.

honestState.p1: This establishes preexistence, not, by itself, full deity — a long step from the popular “man later deified” story. And the live dispute with the strongest skeptic is not “preexistence is late” versus “preexistence is early”: Bart Ehrman takes the earliest Christology to be one of exaltation, yet he also finds a preexistent Christ in material older than Paul; what he denies of that early figure is not his date but his rank — a subordinate being, God’s chief angel or a divinity of a lower order, rather than God. Paul’s creation texts answer that rank question in part: the one by whom every created thing was made cannot himself be one of the created things. The fuller case is made in the divine-identity essays.
honestState.fairness: Several readings are genuinely contested. The pre-Pauline dating of the Philippians hymn is debated (Fee argues Paul composed it), the meaning of harpagmos is one of the most disputed words in the New Testament, and Dunn’s Adam reading is still held by respected scholars — which is why the argument, having answered it on the text, is built to survive even if the hymn is set aside. Wisdom-personification is a genuine part of the background, and “sent,” taken alone, need not imply preexistence.
honestState.verdict: In the earliest Christian writings we possess — letters, and the older confessions they quote — the crucified Jesus is spoken of as one who was sent, who was rich before he was poor, who was in the form of God before he was born, the one through whom the world was made. That is not the language of a man being slowly promoted to heaven. So the answer is yes: Paul’s Christ was personally preexistent. We hold that the one who came down is, as Nicaea confessed, true God from true God — and the one who took a complete human nature to himself without ceasing to be God: full humanity, assumed by one who was already fully God. This argument does not prove that whole confession; it shows that Paul’s Christ came down before he was lifted up, and it places the one who came down on the Creator’s side of creation.

order: Paul’s letters repeatedly present Christ in a downward arc.
Each of these describes a transition from a prior state, or a position outside the created order.
Therefore Paul presents a preexistent Christ.

props.t: the sending named before the birth
the one through whom all things were made
preexistence — a step in the case for Christ’s deity, not the whole of it
a man promoted upward over time

cards.a: Paul’s letters repeatedly present Christ in a downward arc: he is sent from the Father, the sending named before the birth (Galatians 4:4); “though he was rich… became poor” (2 Corinthians 8:9); he was “in the form of God” before “taking the form of a servant” and being “born in the likeness of men” (Philippians 2:6–7); and he is the one “through whom are all things” (1 Corinthians 8:6; Colossians 1:16–17).

cards.q: State Premise 2 — and why the skeptical escapes do not defeat it.
cards.a: Each of these describes a transition from a prior state, or a position outside the created order — not the elevation of a man who began at birth. The skeptical escapes (the Adam reading of the hymn, Wisdom-poetry, “sent” as merely functional) each answer one text; the cumulative pattern, and the named person who is its subject throughout, survive them.

cards.q: What does the conclusion reach — and not reach?
cards.a: That Paul presents a preexistent Christ — one who existed before Bethlehem, who came down and returned, not a man promoted upward over time. It is a step toward the deity of Christ, not identical with it; the full case that he is included in the identity of the one God is made in the divine-identity essays.

cards.q: Why does the order of Galatians 4:4 matter — and what is its limit?
cards.a: God sent his Son, and the Son was then “born of woman.” The sending is named before the birth, which reads awkwardly if the sending simply is the birth of an ordinary man. Limit: taken alone, “sent” need not imply preexistence — prophets are “sent” too — so the weight falls on the cumulative pattern.

cards.q: Why does “he became poor” point to a prior state?
cards.a: The logic is a transition: he was rich, and became poor. A man who was born poor did not “become” poor for anyone’s sake; the sentence presupposes a wealth held before the becoming. It faces its own skeptical reading — a metaphor of earthly self-impoverishment — which is why the case is cumulative.

cards.q: Why is morphē the hinge of Philippians 2:6–7?
cards.a: The same noun describes what he became — a servant — and his servanthood was no costume, so the “form of God” he began in is equally real. And the sequence — in the form of God, then a servant’s form, then born in human likeness — describes a transition from one condition to another.

cards.q: What does “emptied himself” mean — and what does it not mean?
cards.a: The Greek names no thing of which Christ emptied himself — grammatically he emptied himself by taking the form of a servant, by adding humanity, not by subtracting deity. Not that he set aside, lost, or diminished his deity: he remained what he was and became what he was not.

cards.q: What does creation-agency require of the agent?
cards.a: That the agent not be among the created things. The one through whom the world was made stands, by the logic of the claim, before and outside it — the one by whom every created thing was made cannot himself be one of the created things.

cards.q: Reply to: “The creation language is just Wisdom-poetry, not a preexistent person.”
cards.a: Concede that Wisdom-personification is a genuine part of the background. But Wisdom in Proverbs is a poetic personification of an attribute of God; Paul’s Christ is a person with a name, who is “sent,” who “became poor,” who was crucified and raised — a biography, not a personified quality. The motif illuminates the creation language; it does not dissolve the personal subject who undergoes the descent.

cards.q: Which phrase can the Adam reading of Philippians 2 not absorb — and why?
cards.a: “Born in the likeness of men.” To be born in the likeness of men is to come to be human — a transition the first Adam, human from the first, never underwent. A merely human second Adam was never “in the form of God” before “taking the form of a servant” and being “born in the likeness of men.”

cards.q: Concede the Adam reading of the hymn. Does the case fall?
cards.a: No. The same descent shows in other letters: “though he was rich… became poor” reads most naturally as a transition from a prior state, and “through whom are all things” places Christ on the maker’s side of creation. Each faces its own skeptical reading, but those are separate challenges the Adam frame does not supply — so conceding Philippians does not concede the case.

cards.q: A critic grants that Christ preexisted but calls him a subordinate heavenly being. What is the dispute really about — and how far does this case answer it?
cards.a: The dispute is one of kind, not date: not whether the preexistent figure is early, but what rank he holds. This case answers it in part: Paul makes Christ the one through whom all things were made, and the one by whom every created thing was made cannot himself be one of the created things. The fuller case is taken up in the divine-identity essays.

obj.q: Colossians calls Christ “the firstborn of all creation” (1:15) — read plainly, the first and highest creature, made before the rest. And Colossians’ own Pauline authorship is disputed, so even its testimony may be later than Paul.
obj.model: “Firstborn” (prōtotokos) marks priority and rank, not manufacture. Scripture uses it exactly that way of David — “I will make him the firstborn, the highest of the kings of the earth” (Psalm 89:27) — though David was the youngest of Jesse’s sons and, obviously, not literally born first. “Firstborn of all creation” names Christ’s supremacy over creation, and the very next verse blocks the created-being reading: “for by him all things were created” (Colossians 1:16) — the one by whom all created things came to be is not himself one of them. As for authorship: grant the dispute, and the argument does not fall, because the preexistence pattern runs through the letters no one contests Paul wrote — Galatians, 1 Corinthians, 2 Corinthians, Romans, Philippians.

obj.q: You’re reading later doctrine into Paul. The Philippians hymn is Adam Christology: Adam, made in the image of God, grasped at equality with God and was condemned to death; Christ, the last Adam, refused and was exalted. Two men, start to finish — no personal preexistence. The clearest statement of personal preexistence is in John, not Paul.
obj.model: That is James Dunn’s reading, and it is argued from the text, so it is answered on the text. Wright grants the genuine Adam echoes but argues they are woven into a frame the Adam reading cannot carry: a merely human second Adam was never “in the form of God” before “taking the form of a servant” and being “born in the likeness of men.” That last phrase is the one the Adam reading cannot absorb: to be born in the likeness of men is to come to be human, a transition the first Adam, human from the first, never underwent. Fee, more skeptical that the Adam parallel is even in view, adds that morphē theou and morphē doulou resist being flattened into two merely human postures. And the case does not stand on Philippians alone: even granting the Adam reading of the hymn, “became poor” and “through whom are all things” are separate challenges the Adam frame does not supply.

obj.q: Prophets are “sent” without preexisting; a rich man who gives to the poor “becomes poor” without any heavenly wealth. So “sent” is functional and “became poor” describes Jesus’s earthly self-impoverishment. None of it requires that Christ existed before Bethlehem.
obj.model: For “sent” taken alone, the point is granted outright — which is exactly why the argument is cumulative rather than resting on it; but in Galatians 4:4 the sending is named before the birth. And 2 Corinthians 8:9 resists the flattening: “though he was rich… he became poor” is the grammar of a transition, and a man born poor did not “become” poor for anyone’s sake — the sentence presupposes a wealth held before the becoming. No single verse has to carry the case; the same shape recurs — sent, rich-before-poor, in the form of God, agent of creation — and the weight rests on the cumulative pattern, and on the named person who is its subject throughout.

obj.q: Grant the whole downward arc. A figure could preexist his birth and still be a creature — a great angel, a subordinate heavenly being — without being God. Ehrman accepts a preexistent Christ in material older than Paul and reads him exactly that way. So the real question, creature or Creator, is untouched.
obj.model: Scope is owed: this establishes preexistence, not, by itself, full deity — preexistence is a step toward the deity of Christ, not identical with it. That is why the debate is not “late versus early” but a question of rank. But the case answers the rank question in part: Paul makes Christ the one through whom all things were made, and the one by whom every created thing was made cannot himself be one of the created things — so Paul places this preexistent one on the Creator’s side of creation. The fuller case is taken up in the divine-identity essays. And what preexistence does settle is decisive against the popular story: the earliest Christian writer does not present a man slowly promoted to heaven but one who came down.

unseen.q: Read Colossians 1:16 carefully: by him “all other things” were created. Christ made everything else — which means he was the first thing God made, and created the rest. Being the agent of creation doesn’t put him outside creation.
unseen.model: The New World Translation inserts the word “other” in Colossians 1:16–20 — “all other things” — so that Christ creates everything except himself; but “other” is not in the Greek text at those points. Without the inserted word the verse says what it says: “by him all things were created… and in him all things hold together” (Colossians 1:16–17). And whatever else creation-agency implies, it requires that the agent not be among the created things — the one through whom the world was made stands, by the logic of the claim, before and outside it. The one by whom all created things came to be is not himself one of them.
